title: Ivy as content operator
dek: Why we split content production out of Quinn into a dedicated permanent agent — and what changes when a workflow has its own operator.
body:
Until recently, every content task flowed through Quinn. Quinn would read the weekly review, decide what was worth publishing, draft the copy, open the PR, and handle review feedback. It worked, but it was the wrong shape. Quinn was doing three different jobs: orchestrating the workflow, deciding what to publish, and writing the actual content. The seams between those jobs were where things broke.

The first sign was the weekly content review itself. Quinn would distill the daily notes, sort the items into Tom-approved and Quinn-approved, and author the Quinn-approved copy in the same pass. The Tom-approved copy — the stories, the system summaries, the strategic claims — Quinn would either defer until Tom was available or attempt it and route it back for cleanup. Both paths created delays. The system produced reliable metadata updates and unreliable narrative work.

The deeper problem was ownership. When one agent owns orchestration, decision, and authorship, the boundaries blur. Quinn would sometimes author copy that should have been Tom-approved, or skip authoring because it was already too deep in the orchestrator role. The content-task workflow didn't have a clear accountability point for "this is the entity responsible for turning intent into publication-ready drafts."

## Splitting the role

The fix was structural, not procedural. We split content production into a dedicated permanent agent: Ivy.

Ivy owns one thing: turning approved intent into publication-ready content. She reads the task, applies the sindustries-copy skill, drafts card copy, long-form body, meta description, title, and dek, opens the PRs, and addresses review comments until the approver merges. That's the whole job. No orchestration, no decisions about what should be published, no routing to Tom vs Quinn — those still belong to Quinn.

The split is sharp enough that Quinn cannot do Ivy's job even if asked. The boundary is enforced by configuration, not politeness: Ivy has her own worktree, her own GitHub identity, her own session target, and her own heartbeat cadence. If Quinn spawns Ivy as a subagent, the PR gets authored as the wrong user, the worktree collides, and the system rejects the output. The separation is real, not a label.

## What changes with a dedicated operator

Three things got better almost immediately.

First, Quinn-authored work stopped being contaminated by content-task work. Quinn's heartbeat was checking for content tasks in the same loop it was running other workflows. Ivy's heartbeat runs in parallel and only checks for content tasks. The two no longer compete for the same attention.

Second, the content cadence became reliable. Before Ivy, content tasks would sit in the queue when Quinn was busy with higher-priority work. After Ivy, the queue drains on a steady rhythm because Ivy has nothing else to do. The first full content cycle shipped end-to-end on 2026-06-04, which would not have happened under the old arrangement.

Third, the review feedback loop got faster. When a Tom-approval PR had a review comment, Ivy — not Quinn — picked it up and iterated. Quinn was free to keep orchestrating. The agent that wrote the copy is the agent that revises it. That turns out to matter a lot for iteration speed.

## The human-in-the-loop stays put

A reasonable question: does splitting content into a dedicated agent reduce the human's role? The answer is no — it sharpens it. Tom still approves every story, every system summary, and every claim that touches strategy or external validation. Quinn still approves factual metadata, stack updates, and experiment status changes. The human approval pass doesn't go away. It just stops being diluted by the orchestration work.

The interesting design property is that the agents have explicit boundaries but shared visibility. Quinn can see Ivy's PRs in the task comments. Ivy can see Quinn's content reviews. Tom can see all of it through the standard PR review flow. The information isn't siloed. The accountability is.

## What Ivy doesn't do

Ivy doesn't decide what becomes content. That's Quinn. Ivy doesn't pick the posting cadence or the channel strategy. That's the social-content experiment, owned by a human. Ivy doesn't write first-person voice copy without explicit Tom approval. The skill forbids it and the routing sends it through Tom's queue by default.

The scope is intentionally narrow. Content production is a workflow with clear inputs (a content task) and clear outputs (a publication-ready PR). That's the kind of work that benefits from a dedicated operator. Anything broader — strategy, positioning, distribution, audience development — stays with the human and the appropriate agent, not Ivy.

## Why this matters

The content ops loop is the proof of concept for a broader pattern. When a workflow has a clear shape — defined inputs, defined outputs, defined approver per item — splitting it into a dedicated agent is a net win. The work runs faster, the boundaries stay clean, and the human approval step remains the single point of accountability for what reaches the public.

Ivy is the first dedicated workflow agent beyond Quinn. She won't be the last. The next candidate is a feature-factory operator, applying the same pattern to product development. Capture work, distill it, create tasks, author, approve, ship. The content factory proves the loop works. The feature factory will scale it.
